mechanisms.name: Five-layer diffusion, constant diffusivity per layer
mechanisms.status_basis: The BTCS solver (result label COMPUTED v2.0) solves the layered equation by the spherical backward-time central-space finite-difference scheme (Method A) and is compared with the Sturm-Liouville analytical solution (Method B). Conservation in exact arithmetic and positivity are proved for the scheme as specified; the tests show second-order convergence in space, first-order convergence in time, a balance residual within its derived rounding bound and agreement with the analytical solution on the synthetic five-layer case. Numerical verification only: no comparison with measurements exists.

species.summary: Ag-110m, an activation product with a 249.83 d half-life, passes through intact SiC coatings; AGR-1 compacts released from about 0 % to more than 90 % of it.
Palladium has no isotope of radiological consequence but crosses intact SiC and corrodes it, a key contributor to the SiC failures found in AGR-1 particles.
Caesium is effectively retained by intact SiC, so its release measures SiC integrity; Cs-137 is one of the owner's first Phase 2 nuclides.
Strontium passes intact coatings in small amounts and is held in the OPyC and matrix; Sr-90 is one of the owner's first Phase 2 nuclides.
Europium passes intact coatings at levels about ten times those of strontium and is largely held in the OPyC and compact matrix.
Radioiodine is expected to be released like the fission gases through failed coatings; deferred in STRATO because no PyC or SiC iodine diffusivity is registered.
Ruthenium, a noble-metal fission product, was retained even in AGR-1 particles with failed SiC; little transport evidence exists.
Xenon is a fission gas held gas-tight by intact SiC; its release-to-birth ratio monitored AGR-1 for coating failures.
Krypton release indicates TRISO coating failure; Kr-85 is the owner's second Phase 2 nuclide, with a precursor-delay caveat.

Silver moves much faster along SiC grain boundaries than through the grain interiors, so the grain-boundary network, not the crystal lattice, would control silver transport through an intact coating. Fast-neutron damage changes the SiC. In SiC from TRISO particles irradiated in three reactors, the content of caesium, cerium, europium, ruthenium and antimony was proportional to the number of neutrons that had passed through the SiC; the source conjectures that damage from slowing-down neutrons creates sites at which fission products bind, or paths by which they enter the coating

. The FRG caesium diffusivity in SiC carries an empirical fluence factor
Densification of the buffer by fission-product recoil and neutron irradiation is unavoidable at the burnup and dose of AGR-1

. In the particle model of PARFUME the pyrocarbon layers shrink and creep under irradiation: early in irradiation their shrinkage puts the SiC in compression, creep later relieves it, and the growing fission-gas pressure puts the layers in tension; a pressure-vessel failure occurs if the tangential stress in the SiC exceeds the strength of that particle's SiC
. PARFUME also treats multi-dimensional behaviour seen in examinations: radial cracking of the IPyC, partial debonding of the IPyC from the SiC, aspherical particles and the amoeba effect

c.v: Palladium-assisted degradation of SiC (Pd-SiC and Ag-Pd interactions)

Brick 6. Species: Pd (the attacking species) and Ag (the species whose transport palladium may assist). Material domain: the SiC layer. Regime B (palladium-assisted migration, Pd-SiC chemical interaction, microstructural degradation); a layer penetrated by palladium is a failed barrier, which is Regime C. Every equation below is a research concept, not solved by STRATO.

Fission-product palladium reaches the IPyC-SiC interface and reacts with silicon carbide. Chemical attack by palladium is described as transforming SiC into a mixture of palladium silicide and graphite

. Ab initio molecular dynamics at 2000 K shows palladium atoms disintegrating a SiC surface and removing carbon into chain-like structures, while silver atoms are repelled from the surface; the authors suggest that palladium attack is an important first step in silver diffusion through SiC

items.v: Penetration of the SiC by palladium thins the barrier. Complete penetration provides an open path for fission products and is a functional failure of the particle; local thinning contributes little to stress-driven failure, while thinning over large areas can cause failure through stress concentrations and IPyC failure

Neethling, Olivier and O'Connell proposed that palladium penetrates SiC grain boundaries, forms palladium silicides, and that silver joins them in Ag-rich Pd-Ag-Si nodules that migrate along boundaries by dissolving SiC at the leading edge and reprecipitating it at the trailing edge; only small palladium concentrations would be needed, and high-temperature neutron irradiation would accelerate the process

. As reported by a DOE-funded study, Ag-Pd transport was significantly enhanced in high-temperature, high-dose neutron-irradiated 3C-SiC, but it is unclear whether this holds for silver without palladium
. The original papers (

Palladium crossed intact SiC

In particles that released caesium during irradiation, the IPyC had cracked and the exposed SiC had suffered concentrated palladium attack; SiC failures after safety testing at 1600 to 1800 °C were related to fabrication defects or to extensive palladium corrosion where the SiC was exposed by similar IPyC cracks

c.v: The STRATO research catalogue sorts proposed physics into three transport regimes. They are transport regimes, not mutually exclusive mechanisms: one particle can show several at once, and a mechanism can move a particle from one regime to another. Regime A covers transport through coating layers that are structurally intact, with the barrier properties the layers had when made, changed only by the diffusing species themselves.

STRATO's present model, five-layer diffusion with a constant diffusivity per layer, is the simplest Regime A description: each layer is treated as a homogeneous medium with one effective diffusivity. The mechanisms below are what such an effective diffusivity hides.
Note on names: Harrison's kinetic types A, B and C for grain-boundary diffusion, used in some sources
, are a different classification from STRATO's regimes A, B and C.

items.v: For silver in ideal 3C-SiC every defect state has a very high activation energy, about 7.9 eV for the fastest (the interstitial), so bulk transport is very slow

. High-energy boundaries modelled as amorphous SiC give still faster diffusion

: the evidence conflicts.

items.v: Density-functional calculations for ideal 3C-SiC give very high activation energies for every silver defect state; the lowest, for the silver interstitial, is about 7.9 eV, so bulk transport is very slow and another path must operate

Silver defect formation energies are 2 to 4 eV lower in a Σ3 grain boundary than in the bulk, a strong tendency to segregate; at 1600 °C the predicted Σ3 and bulk diffusion coefficients are 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁸ and 3.9 × 10⁻²⁹ m² s⁻¹

Nano-sized (about 2 to 5 nm) silver precipitates were found in SiC grain boundaries and triple points, none inside grains

Caesium is the species whose retention best shows whether the SiC layer is intact. Past experience with TRISO fuel shows that the SiC layer is the primary containment of caesium, so caesium release is an effective indicator of SiC failure; caesium diffuses with relative ease through intact pyrocarbon but is effectively retained by intact SiC
. Caesium and strontium both have isotopes that would be radiologically hazardous if released after an accident in a reactor using TRISO fuel

In the AGR-1 irradiation the Cs-134 fractional release from the compacts was below 3 × 10⁻⁶ in the four capsules whose particles all kept intact SiC, and about 10⁻⁵ in the two capsules that held particles with failed SiC; an estimated four of about 2.98 × 10⁵ particles failed their SiC in pile, an in-pile SiC failure fraction of 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ (at most 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ at 95 % confidence)

. In the post-irradiation safety tests at 1600 to 1800 °C, caesium release from compacts without failed SiC stayed below 5 × 10⁻⁶ after 300 h at 1600 °C or 100 h at 1800 °C, and the overall caesium release was dominated by the SiC defect and failure fractions

Radioiodine is a safety-relevant fission product. In TRISO fuel its release is expected to follow that of the fission gases: the release of fission gases and iodine from coated particles is widely expected to be directly correlated with a defective or failed coating, an intact SiC layer keeps the particle gas-tight, and an intact OPyC significantly delays gaseous fission products that have passed the SiC; it has been standard practice, supported by experimental evidence, to assume that fission gases and iodine show a similar release behaviour under accident conditions

The owner deferred I-131 from the first Phase 2 nuclides (owner decision D1, 2026-11-24) because the parameter register holds no PyC or SiC iodine diffusivity. Caesium, strontium and krypton come first.
